newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German banks retreat on unpopular sick pay cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German banks retreat on unpopular sick pay cut.

text.p: German bank employers on Monday said they would postpone making a controversial cut to sick payments until a wider wage agreement had been reached for the more than 450,000 workers in the sector.

The decision is the second major blow in two days for a deeply unpopular law introduced by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government in October, allowing employers to cut sick pay from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.
Employers in the metal and engineering sector said on Sunday that they saw little chance of implementing the law following mass worker protests against it.
Representatives of banking employers stressed that they, however, had not yet given up on making the cuts.
"Today we have decided not to make a decision," Horst Mueller of the German Private Bank Employers Federation told a news briefing held jointly with banking unions.
Union officials, however, declared the decision an "intermediate success".
"In our view it is a success because banking employees from today will get their 100 percent sick pay back," Klaus Carlin of the HBV banking trade union said.
Carlin said protests in the sector would as a result be temporarily suspended.

Last month more than 15,000 German bank employees took to the streets to protest against the cut to sick payments made by most of the major commercial banks including Deutsche Bank AG , the country's largest bank.

The banking sector had been the only large industry in Germany where employers have acted together to enforce the law, which was part of an austerity package introduced by Bonn to ensure German entry to the single European currency in 1999.

Germany's banks had said they have been little affected by industrial action by bank workers, which has been relatively limited compared to protests involving hundreds of thousands of engineering workers.

But the worsening of relations in the German banking sector, which has not seen widespread industrial action since 1992, comes as the major banks are seeking to win more business by extending opening hours.
That is expected to mean requiring employees to work more overtime -- something that many bank staff are already refusing to do as a result of the cuts to sick pay.
Further talks in the bank sector are now due to be held in late January 1997.
